transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-05 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Evelyn Hart (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Cerulean), Tomaz Kline (Cerulean), Leah Wu (Cerulean)

Summary: Quick pre-handoff technical deep dive for air-gapped delivery. Covered artifact signing/checksums, offline license handshake options, GPU driver compat, kernel module quirks, and runtime warmup (KV cache + batching) impacts on latency. Agreed on signed manifest approach and next steps for on-site handoff window.

Topics: artifact packaging, checksum verification, cosign/signed-manifest, offline activation tokens, hostID binding, GPU driver matrix, kernel module modprobe timing, DKMS vs prebuilt modules, KV cache warmup strategies, continuous batching parameters, quantization profile impacts on cold-start latency.

Transcript:
[00:00:03] Evelyn: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Evelyn from Redwood. We wanted to run through the actual offline bootstrap path and the things we'll need from you to create the sealed images and the offline license. Marco will cover the driver stuff and I can walk through the signed manifest and license handshake.
[00:00:17] Priya: yep thanks Evelyn, appreciate it. Our primary ask here is a reproducible, auditable offline process — we can't have nodes phone home, and security wants host-bound licenses and verifiable artifact integrity.
[00:00:30] Marco: cool, and we kinda assume you'll be doing a sneakernet transfer, right? USB-to-locked-laptop or tape, depending on the datacenter ops.
[00:00:36] Leah: yes, sneakernet with encrypted containers is our plan. We also have a requirement that we can validate manifests without Redwood's online services.
[00:00:44] Tomaz: and SOC2 controls mean audit logs and signed manifests are must-haves.
[00:00:48] Evelyn: perfect. So first piece: artifact signing. Our recommended flow is a signed manifest (we use cosign in hosted flows) that contains sha256 digests for each bundle piece — runtime binaries, docker images (if entombed), kernel modules, and the license blob. The receiver can verify signature with your public key and verify the sha256 checksums locally.
[00:01:06] Leah: quick Q — can the manifest include per-file chunk checksums? We sometimes need to validate large images where a single corruption byte should be obvious.
[00:01:14] Marco: yeah you can include chunked sha256 ranges, speaking from the se side. We often create a chunk map for large artifacts — it just makes validation streaming-friendly on low-RAM nodes.
[00:01:24] Tomaz: and how do we handle the signed license? Do we get a pre-signed activation token tied to hostID?
[00:01:30] Evelyn: there are two patterns we support. Option A: host-bound license files — you provide hostIDs (MAC + hardware UUID; we support multiple idents) and we produce a signed license file that expires per your contract. Option B: ephemeral activation token — we provide an offline activation challenge/response tool where you run the challenge on the target, produce a challenge file, send it back via secure courier, we sign and return an activation response file. Both are offline-friendly.
[00:01:52] Priya: we prefer host-bound if possible — avoids extra courier round trips. We'll need to validate that the license can't be trivially rehosted.
[00:02:00] Marco: license files are signed with our private key (RSA 4096 currently) and include the allowed model set, expiration, and a binding fingerprint of provided hostIDs. On boot the runtime verifies the signature using the public key embedded in the runtime image. If hostID mismatches we refuse to load the model blobs.
[00:02:18] Leah: does the runtime verify the license before loading quantized artifacts or after? Because big quant artifacts can take time to copy into the local cache.
[00:02:25] Marco: good question — we verify license before any heavy disk IO. So the handshake happens early, we check signature and host binding, then proceed to unpack models. That avoids wasted IO if the license is invalid.
[00:02:36] Tomaz: on the driver side, what versions are supported? We have a mix of 525 and 535 series kernels in staging.
[00:02:42] Marco: we support a matrix: nvidia-driver 525+, 530, 535; runtime modules expect the nvidia-uvm and nvidia modules available. We recommend using our prebuilt kernel module tarball for 525/530 kernels to avoid DKMS pain. However, if you use DKMS we provide a build hook script.
[00:02:58] Leah: any firmware restrictions? One node hit an ECC firmware bug last month.
[00:03:02] Marco: we do check GPU firmware against a compatibility table; we'll share the table. The big gotcha is kernel ABI mismatches when using older distro kernels with newer driver bundles. We'll run compatibility tests for your specific kernel versions.
[00:03:15] Evelyn: also note that our offline package includes a small kernel module loader helper — it runs a modprobe sequence and validates /proc/driver/nvidia entries. Sometimes modprobe ordering affects udev rules and the nvidia-uvm device node creation.
[00:03:29] Tomaz: great, please send that helper. We want deterministic logs for our change control.
[00:03:33] Evelyn: absolutely. Next topic: checksums and signed manifests. Our sample manifest will be a JSON-ish manifest where each path has a sha256, size, and optionally chunked ranges. The manifest itself is signed. We'll provide a small verifier binary (static) that can run on air-gapped nodes and verify both the signature and the underlying digests.
[00:03:50] Leah: will that verifier use OpenSSL? We need FIPS compatibility in some envs.
[00:03:55] Marco: the verifier is built against BoringSSL by default but we can produce a FIPS-compatible build or provide a minimal verification script using openssl if needed.
[00:04:05] Priya: on runtime perf, our big concern is cold start latency. With quantized models and cold KV cache, customers see big latency spikes on first queries. How do you recommend warmups?
[00:04:14] Marco: we typically do a two-stage warmup. Stage 1: eager KV prefetch — we unpack and prepopulate the key/value cache with frequent prompt prefixes. Stage 2: batched synthetic traces — we run a set of synthetic sequences at production batch sizes to warm JIT paths and kernels. For airgapped setups we include a warmup script that uses a supplied prompt corpus to populate the cache.
[00:04:34] Leah: does that script respect licensing limits? We don't want it to accidentally consume license-limited tokens.
[00:04:39] Evelyn: the warmup script uses internal admin endpoints that bypass token metering for warmup only — for the offline flow the license file contains a warmup allowance flag so the runtime won't treat warmup as billable.
[00:04:51] Tomaz: what about KV eviction policies? We've seen KV thrash when we have long-tail sessions.
[00:04:56] Marco: our runtime supports LRU with size caps and time-to-idle. For long conversational workloads we recommend adaptive eviction tuned to sequence length profiles. If you have very long contexts, you might use prefix-only persistence for certain sessions and full KV for hot sessions. We include a tuning guide.
[00:05:12] Priya: batching — your default recommends continuous batching. In locked datacenter environments we sometimes prefer fixed batch sizing to reduce jitter. Any tradeoffs?
[00:05:20] Marco: continuous batching reduces tokens/sec cost but increases tail latency variance. For SLO-sensitive API surfaces you can pin batch size and use a latency SLO controller that will prioritize small batches under high tail latency. The control is per-route so you can mix modes.
[00:05:34] Leah: quantization — is there a recommended profile for 4-bit quant for our workloads? We mostly do short replies but high QPS.
[00:05:40] Marco: 4-bit quantization (QLoRA-style or our proprietary 4bit-fused kernels) gives significant memory reduction with modest perf delta. For short replies at high QPS we usually recommend 4-bit with tensor remapping enabled and cache preallocation to avoid on-the-fly allocations. We'll share recommended quant profiles for your model family.
[00:05:56] Tomaz: any implications for cold-start? I assume more quantized artifacts unpack faster but may need kernel tuning.
[00:06:01] Marco: right — quantized artifacts are smaller so unpack is faster, but some kernels use different GEMM kernels which can JIT at runtime; warmup scripts handle that by triggering those code paths.
[00:06:11] Priya: around verification — we want to ensure the signed manifest verification is replay-safe. If an attacker swaps a file but keeps size the same how are we protected?
[00:06:19] Marco: the manifest protects by using sha256 over file bytes — changing content changes the digest. For streaming, chunk checksums catch partial corruption. The signature prevents an attacker from producing a new manifest unless they have the signing key.
[00:06:30] Leah: and the signing key is held by Redwood? Do we have an option for customer-side signing?
[00:06:34] Evelyn: both supported. Many customers prefer us to sign (we use a per-contract key) but you can also bring your own signing key — we'll trust a customer public key embedded in the verifier. That way Cerulean can sign artifacts internally.
[00:06:46] Tomaz: okay good. On the offline license format — can we get a machine-readable proof for audits, like a signed assertion list with timestamps?
[00:06:54] Evelyn: yes, licenses include issuance timestamp, signing cert fingerprint, permitted model IDs, node bindings, and an audit URL field which we populate with a time-stamped receipt. For fully offline audits we can produce a signed audit bundle at handoff time.
[00:07:08] Priya: network isolation concern — we need the control plane to be fully offline. Does the runtime require any outbound network at runtime for telemetry?
[00:07:15] Marco: no, in Private/Airgapped mode telemetry is disabled by default. If you choose to enable it later we provide an opt-in agent that will buffer and forward via a secure gateway.
[00:07:24] Leah: deployment checklist please — what exactly goes on the USB? We want a canonical list.
[00:07:29] Evelyn: checklist we suggest: signed manifest (manifest.json.sig), all artifact blobs (model.q4, runtime.tgz, driver-module.tar), verifier binary, license file (if pre-bound), kernel module helper, warmup script and warmup corpus, release notes, and an integrity checklist (sha256sum file). We'll provide a sample packaging script that creates the bundle and a step-by-step install runbook.
[00:07:47] Tomaz: for kernel modules — is it better to use DKMS or prebuilt modules? We prefer no builds in datacenter.
[00:07:52] Marco: prebuilt modules packaged against your kernel versions are simpler; DKMS can fail due to missing build deps. For the airgapped flow we recommend prebuilt modules. We also provide an offline fallback that uses retpoline-safe shim modules if your kernel prohibits certain ops.
[00:08:06] Priya: about activation — if we lose a node and want to revoke license, what's the offline revoke story?
[00:08:12] Evelyn: offline revocation is handled by short duration licenses plus a signed revocation list distributed at next maintenance window. Also, we support ephemeral activation tokens for nodes you expect to rotate often. For strong revocation you can set very short TTLs and require periodic physical reactivation.
[00:08:24] Leah: okay we also want to run a benchmark — can we run your stress harness on-prem?
[00:08:29] Marco: yes, we include a benchmark harness that runs latency and throughput sweeps, KV-warmup tests, prefix loads, and quantized vs fp16 comparisons. It outputs CSVs and a simple dashboard. We'll need to confirm it doesn't require outbound telemetry.
[00:08:41] Evelyn: it doesn't. The harness is self-contained. It creates local perf traces and you can share results via secure courier or upload to our portal later.
[00:08:49] Tomaz: any gotchas for container runtimes? We run older containerd in some racks.
[00:08:54] Marco: containerd <1.6 might have issues with snapshotters and big opaque blobs. For those nodes we provide a tarball install path that unpacks directly to the filesystem and runs the runtime as a systemd service.
[00:09:05] Leah: will the runtime run in rootless mode?
[00:09:08] Marco: currently we recommend rootful for performance and device node access; rootless is experimental due to GPU device access complexities.
[00:09:16] Priya: can we get the lab to do a rehearsed install with one of our images?
[00:09:20] Marco: yes, we'll take one of your kernel images and reproduce the install in our lab. That's on Marco's action item.
[00:09:25] Evelyn: quick recap before we wrap: we'll share signed-manifest tooling and sample manifests, the kernel module helper, the warmup scripts and corpus, and the benchmark harness. Cerulean will provide hostIDs and target nodes list. We'll schedule a 2-hour on-site handoff window for the physical transfer and a subsequent lab validation.
[00:09:42] Tomaz: sounds good. Any blockers from Redwood side?
[00:09:45] Marco: none. We'll need the hostIDs and the kernel images to run the compatibility checks.
[00:09:50] Priya: we'll get that to you by EOD next Tuesday.
[00:09:55] Evelyn: perfect, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the package and runbook and propose times for the handoff.
[00:10:02] Leah: thanks.
[00:10:04] meeting end — rest of calls were wrap-up and scheduling notes.

Notes on transcript quality: automatic transcription had occasional errors around kernel names and product names like "cosign" was rendered as "co-sign" and "nvidia-uvm" sometimes came through as "nvidia uvm". Speaker turns occasionally overlap, and timestamps are approximate.

References/links mentioned: sample-manifest repo (internal link to be shared), signed-manifest tooling (cosign), kernel-compat matrix (will be shared as spreadsheet).

End of transcript.
